The Story of Lakshmimati

I bow to Lord Jinendra, whose knowledge illuminates the world and beyond, and through whose knowledge all things are known. For the sake of one's own welfare, I bow to that Lord and write a story about pride.

In the beautiful village named Lakshmi in the land of Magadh, there lived a Brahmin named Somsharma. His wife was Lakshmimati — beautiful, in the prime of youth, endowed with many virtues, but with one flaw: she was deeply proud of her caste and spent her days absorbed in adorning herself.

One day, after observing a fifteen-day fast, the great monk Shri Samadhi Gupt came to their house for alms. Somsharma seated the monk with devotion on a high seat and, asking his wife to serve the meal, went out on some urgent business. The Brahmini sat looking at her own face in a mirror. Filled with pride, she hurled abuses at the monk, spoke ill of him, and shut the door. Alas! What greater sin could there be? The monk was peaceful, an ocean of austerity, devoted to the welfare of all, endowed with many virtues and high conduct — so he paid no heed to the Brahmini's wickedness and simply departed. Truly, even the treasure that comes to the house of sinners departs.

From the sin of reviling a monk, leprosy broke out on Lakshmimati's body on the seventh day. Her condition worsened, and the family cast her out of the house. Unable to bear suffering upon suffering, she sat in fire and burned to death. She died in terrible states of mind. From that sin she was reborn as a donkey in the same village, in a washerman's house. In that state she could not even get milk to drink. She died and was reborn as a sow. Then twice she took birth as a dog. In one of those lives she perished in a forest fire. Now she was born as a one-eyed girl named Kana in a boatman's family in Bhrigukachchh village on the banks of the Narmada. Her body stank from birth, and no one wished to sit near her. See the fruit of pride — Lakshmimati was a Brahmini, yet through her arrogance she fell to the lowest birth.

Eventually, through the ripening of merit, she was freed from those lower births and regained human form. She remembered her past lives and the terrible cost of her pride and reviling of saints. She took refuge in the Jain dharma, practised charity, worship, and vows, and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that pride — especially pride in birth, beauty, or caste — is a poison that leads to ruin. And reviling saints brings swift and terrible consequences. The wise should cultivate humility and guard their tongue, for these are the foundations of spiritual progress.
